entry.title: Pixels & Parcels - Managing New Mexico's Water with Landsat

media:group.media:title: Pixels & Parcels - Managing New Mexico's Water with Landsat
media:group.media:description:
When water is scarce, knowing exactly how it’s been used can make all the difference. In New Mexico, one of the driest states in the U.S., the state’s Office of the State Engineer partnered with NASA to bring a half-century of Landsat satellite data to bear on that challenge — building the Water ET Reporting Tool: a system that lets water managers pull up any parcel of land and see exactly how much water was used, month by month, going back to the 1980s. What once took weeks of detective work now takes a fraction of the time — helping protect agriculture, reduce wildfire risk, and ensure that in a place where every drop counts, decisions are made with the best possible information.
Learn more: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/landsat/benefits/water-resources/

entry.title: Hubble and Roman: A Partnership 36 Years in the Making

media:group.media:title: Hubble and Roman: A Partnership 36 Years in the Making
media:group.media:description:
Two powerful space telescopes. Two unique views of the universe. One shared mission of discovery.
NASA’s Hubble and Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescopes are designed to explore the cosmos in different but complementary ways. While Roman will survey vast regions of space to uncover new insights into dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, Hubble will provide detailed observations that help scientists better understand these discoveries.
Learn how these two telescopes will work together to unlock new mysteries of the universe and usher in a new era of astronomical discovery.
For more information, visit science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble

entry.title: How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds

media:group.media:title: How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
media:group.media:description:
The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. New studies explore how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy.
The most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits. If an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way we’ll be able to uncover.
The LISA detection method is similar to one called radial velocity that uses light and is already employed to find exoplanets around nearby stars. As a planet orbits, its gravity tugs on its host star, imparting a small reflex motion, or wobble, onto it. This wobble causes the star’s spectrum to oscillate, with spectral lines shifting from redder wavelengths as the star moves away from us to bluer ones as the star moves toward us. The shift is due to a phenomenon called the Doppler effect.
Something similar occurs with gravitational waves. By themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency. Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal. For LISA, this modulation will appear as sidebands, secondary signals at both higher and lower frequencies than the primary one.
Scientists liken the situation to modern radio communication, where some of the energy of a main radio carrier frequency goes into forming sidebands at adjacent upper and lower frequencies that carry messages (like voices or music). For gravitational waves, the sidebands carry messages about the presence of a planet.
Using this technique for a test case system at a distance of 500 light-years, researchers have found that LISA could detect a sub-Jupiter exoplanet under ideal circumstances. Music credit: “A Light Left Burning” Lukas Knoebl [SESAC], Universal Production Music

media:group.media:title: NASA, NOAA 2026 Ozone Hole Update
media:group.media:description:
Earth’s protective ozone layer remains on track for long-term recovery, despite atmospheric conditions that contributed to a larger Antarctic ozone hole in 2026, NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reported. The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but was not as deep as other large holes on record.

media:group.media:title: Giant Cosmic Cat Spotted!
media:group.media:description:
Pspspsp! Just in time for Halloween, NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7,500 light-years away from Earth.
The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the “magical” process of star formation.
Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details.
For more information, visit science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble

entry.title: Why The Universe Doesn’t Add Up (And How We’re Going To Try To Figure It Out)

media:group.media:title: Why The Universe Doesn’t Add Up (And How We’re Going To Try To Figure It Out)
media:group.media:description:
For decades, NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has helped astronomers measure how fast the universe is expanding. But as those measurements have become more precise, scientists have uncovered a cosmic mystery: the universe appears to be expanding at different rates depending on how we measure it.
Known as the Hubble tension, this discrepancy challenges our understanding of the cosmos and could point toward something missing from our current model of the universe.
In this video, NASA scientists Jennifer Wiseman and Julie McEnery explore how Hubble helped transform our understanding of cosmic expansion, the mysterious role of dark energy, and how NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will help investigate some of the biggest unanswered questions in cosmology.
For more information, visit science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble

media:group.media:title: Goddard Glossary: Terminator
media:group.media:description:
Let's step into the light and explore the terminator.
It's the line between day and night. As the Artemis II crew flew over the Moon's terminator, they saw lunar craters and ridges cast dramatic shadows, the kind future explorers might see at the Moon's South Pole.
The Artemis II Preliminary Science Report dropped last week, with hundreds of gigabytes of crew observations. From the rugged shadows at the edge of the terminator to a solar eclipse from the far side of the Moon, the science report is full of new details to explore.

media:group.media:title: The Science of Smoke Illustrated
media:group.media:description:
Smoke is not a monolithic thing. Smoke is a mixture of gases, liquids, and primarily particles, which are also known as aerosols. PACE is gathering data on these aerosols so that we can get a better picture of how smoke interacts with the atmosphere, and all kinds of far-reaching effects. The data from PACE will help inform wildfire models, but also give us a general better sense of how aerosols from smoke impact things like air quality, human health, weather, cloud formation and other aspects of how our planet Earth works.

entry.title: Dying Star Creates Brand New Planet

media:group.media:title: Dying Star Creates Brand New Planet
media:group.media:description:
What if a star’s death could give rise to an entirely new planet?
Astronomers revisiting decades-old observations from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope found an unexpected chemical clue around a white dwarf: niobium, a heavy element forged during the final stages of a star’s life.
Combined with observations from other NASA missions, the evidence points to an intriguing possibility: a Jupiter-sized world may have formed from material expelled when the star died.
If confirmed, this “second-generation” planet could reveal that the death of a star isn’t always the end of its planetary system. Sometimes, it might be the beginning of a new one.
For more information, visit science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble

media:group.media:title: Goddard Glossary: Albedo
media:group.media:description:
Let's reflect...
Albedo is a measure of how much light and heat a surface reflects. Lighter objects tend to have higher albedo, and darker objects have lower. This reflectivity plays an important role in studying the makeup of the surface of bodies like the Moon.
Studying the albedo of lighter and darker patches on the Moon — with crew observations from missions like Artemis II, and spacecraft like LRO — helps us to identify types of rocks present in different regions, and the likely history of their formation.
Albedo matters a lot back on Earth, too! The brighter surfaces of clouds and ice help reflect light from the Sun back into space, which plays a crucial role in keeping our planet a comfortable temperature to support life.

media:group.media:title: NASA Will Explore Asteroid Apophis
media:group.media:description:
OSIRIS-APEX is NASA’s mission to study the physical changes to asteroid Apophis that will result from its rare close encounter with Earth in April 2029. That year, Apophis’ orbit will bring it within 20,000 miles (32,000 kilometers) of Earth’s surface – closer to Earth than our highest-altitude satellites. Our planet’s gravitational pull is expected to alter the asteroid’s orbit, change how fast it spins on its axis, and possibly cause quakes or landslides that will modify its surface. The OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft will observe these changes as it passes by Earth within an hour of Apophis, on track for a rendezvous with the asteroid in mid-2029.
Learn more: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/osiris-apex/

entry.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launches!

media:group.media:title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launches!
media:group.media:description:
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope successfully lifted off from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, at 7:26 a.m. EDT (1126 UTC) on August 30, 2026.
The telescope is destined for Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2 (L2), about 1 million miles away where it will transform our understanding of the universe.
This video includes highlights from the exciting day of launch.
Learn more at: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/

entry.title: Tiny Worlds Discovered by Hubble and Webb

media:group.media:title: Tiny Worlds Discovered by Hubble and Webb
media:group.media:description:
Beyond Neptune, countless frozen worlds have orbited the Sun for billions of years, preserving clues from the earliest days of our solar system.
By combining observations from NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, astronomers discovered previously unknown Trans-Neptunian Objects, or TNOs, in the deepest search for these distant objects ever conducted.
Together, Hubble and Webb are giving scientists a new look at some of the solar system’s oldest survivors and revealing new clues about how the building blocks of planets, including Earth, first formed.
For more information, visit science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble
